summary.summary: Hammersmith and Fulham borrowed a further £35m from the PWLB and repaid £16m in 2024/25, lifting debt from £269.2m to £288.3m (all fixed rate, average 3.75%), with 82.4% of the debt serviced by the housing account. The striking move is on the other side of the balance sheet: cash invested fell 72% in the year, from £159.3m to £44.2m, all now held short-term in money market funds and one £10m local-authority deposit. The total CFR rose from £614m to £766.7m, so the council is heavily under-borrowed (HRA internal borrowing alone is £222m) and future capital spend implies substantial further borrowing. All prudential indicators were met, with only 2% of debt maturing within 12 months, and the figures remain subject to external audit.

signals.headline: Debt up £19.1m to £288.3m in 2024/25 (£35m new PWLB less £16m repaid) while total CFR rose £152.7m to £766.7m
signals.why: The gap between a £767m borrowing need and £288m actual debt is a pipeline of future borrowing at today's higher rates.

signals.headline: Cash invested fell from £159.3m to £44.2m during 2024/25, all short-term, against £288.3m debt and £235m in-year capital spend
signals.why: A £115m cash rundown in one year leaves a thin buffer and points to external borrowing or further drawdown ahead.

news_drafts.headline: Hammersmith and Fulham schools-funding deficit reached £7.882m, forecast £17.5m by March 2027
news_drafts.lead:
Hammersmith and Fulham's deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) rose to £7.882m at the end of 2025/26 and is forecast to reach £17.5m by 31 March 2027, a rise of £9.618m. The council's annual audit report, put to its Audit Committee on 24 September, attributes this mainly to increased demand in high needs (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities).

The council says it is eligible for the government's High Needs Stability Grant, which supports up to 90% of such deficits. Expected grant totals £16.237m, leaving the council to fund £1.263m from a reserve set up for the purpose. That depends on the Department for Education approving the council's Local SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) Reform Plan, which the council submitted by the deadline. Approval is pending. The council's risk report records the same position: if the plan is approved, 90% of the deficit will be funded through the grant.

The council's statement of accounts (its formal annual accounts) says that, in common with other London boroughs, high needs spending "has been significantly higher than the funding provided by central government". Separately, the risk report says the council achieved the highest available rating in its recent SEND inspection.

findings.headline: Council is current on external audit with no backlog; recent LGA Independent Peer Review concluded H&F is 'a financially well-managed authority with strong track record of sound financial planning'
findings.detail: The council's audit position is clean with no outstanding audit work. A recent independent peer review from the Local Government Association endorsed H&F's financial management and recognised the Ruthless Financial Efficiency programme, which has delivered £156m in savings since 2014. The peer team noted that "the Council's consistent focus on its RFE value has enabled it to meet savings targets while funding key political priorities."
findings.matters: Clean audit status and independent external validation of financial management provide assurance on controls and governance at a time of significant financial stress; the £156m track record demonstrates savings delivery capability.
findings.figures: £156m savings delivered since 2014 under RFE programme
findings.quote: H&F is also up to date on the external audit of its accounts, with no backlog outstanding work.

findings.headline: Uncommitted reserves forecast at £66m by start of 2027/28; paper signals likely increased pressure on reserves to smooth structural funding changes
findings.detail: The council holds approximately £66m in uncommitted reserves at the start of 2027/28, which the paper notes "would normally be considered a reasonable level." However, the report states that "with the funding landscape now having materially changed, there is likely to be additional pressure on our reserves to smooth the impact." The paper explicitly confirms that reserves are not a sustainable solution to recurring budget deficits and will be reserved for one-off projects and unexpected events.
findings.matters: Reserves provide a window for managing transition but are a finite resource; the council's own assessment that reserves will face increased pressure suggests they may fall below prudent levels if the structural deficit is not addressed through other means.
findings.quote: The Council's uncommitted reserves balances are forecast to be approximately £66m by the start of 2027/28, after taking account of forecast in-year budget pressures and Collection Fund balances. This would normally be considered a reasonable level of reserves to manage in-year pressures that may arise, going forward.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit reached £7.9m at end 2025/26, forecast to reach £36.8m cumulative; depends on unconfirmed stability grant covering £33.6m
findings.detail: The High Needs deficit has grown despite a previous Safety Valve agreement (£20.5m to 2024/25). The council forecasts a cumulative unfunded deficit of £36.8m across the MTFS period. Financial planning assumes a stability grant will cover 90% of eligible deficits (£33.6m), leaving a residual risk of £3.2m. The paper explicitly flags this as "a material financial risk" because the stability grant "has not yet been confirmed or received" — if it fails to materialise, the residual would have to be funded from General Fund reserves, impacting the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: An unconfirmed material grant creates financial uncertainty; DSG deficits constrain financial flexibility and are a known pressure point for councils where central policy (SEND funding) outpaces available resources.
findings.figures: Cumulative unfunded deficit 2025/26-2027/28: £36.8m; assumed stability grant coverage: £33.6m (90%); residual council-funded risk: £3.2m
findings.quote: The cumulative unfunded deficit at the end of 2025/26 was £7.9m and the latest 2026/27 forecast is £9.6m, meaning an expected cumulative deficit of £17.5m at the end of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Business rates tariff paid to government increased from £12.8m to £53.6m (quadrupled); H&F's retained rates reduced to £32.7m from ~£86.3m under previous regime
findings.detail: On an initial gross business rates estimate of £301.3m for 2026/27, the council's tariff payment to government has more than quadrupled. This leaves H&F retaining only £32.7m, approximately 10% of initial gross rates, compared to a much higher share under the previous system. The paper explicitly states this is "a very difficult position for H&F to justify to businesses within the borough" and runs counter to the inclusive economic growth strategy.
findings.matters: The dramatic reduction in retained business rates limits the council's ability to benefit from local economic growth, affects its financial relationship with local business, and reduces a key flexible revenue source.
findings.figures: Tariff 2025/26: £12.8m; Tariff 2026/27: £53.6m; Retained rates: £32.7m; Previous regime would have retained ~£86.3m on same gross
findings.quote: This tariff has more than quadrupled from the old regime in 2025/26 (when it was £12.8m) to Fair Funding in 2026/27, (£53.6m).

findings.headline: Government grants H&F unlimited council tax flexibility for 2027/28 and 2028/29; modelled scenarios show 150% increase would 'broadly balance' four-year budget
findings.detail: Three scenarios modelled. A 100% increase (from £1,009 to £2,018 Band D) generates £113.2m cumulative income by 2030/31 but leaves £46.1m gap. A 125% increase generates £138.7m (£20.6m residual gap). A 150% increase (to £2,522.50 Band D, equivalent to £29.11 per week for residents) generates £163.9m and "broadly balances the budget on current assumptions" assuming 5% increases in subsequent years. No other council outside London has been granted this flexibility.
findings.matters: The government's grant of exceptional tax flexibility signals that rates must rise substantially, and future borrowing and financial planning assumptions should reflect the likelihood of major resident-facing increases.
findings.figures: 100% increase: £1,009 annual, £113.2m cumulative income, £46.1m residual gap; 125%: £1,261.25 annual, £138.7m income, £20.6m gap; 150%: £1,513.50 annual (£29.11/week), £163.9m income, broadly balanced
findings.quote: A 150% increase in the H&F council tax element (£2,522.50 a year at Band D) would bring in additional income by 2030/31 of £163.9m – this broadly balances the budget on current assumptions.

daily_post.headline: Fund identified medium-level risk that inadequate cash could force below-market asset sales to meet pension payments
daily_post.lead: Liquidity pressure could force the Fund to crystallise losses by selling assets during market downturns, damaging long-term returns and potentially creating pressure for higher council contributions to recover funding levels.
